title: Explain the classic quadratic bottom-up tabulation for the Longest Increasing Subsequence, how each cell is built from earlier cells, how to reconstruct the actual subsequence with predecessor pointers, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: LIS Tabulation (Quadratic Bottom-Up and Reconstructing the Sequence)

s1_definition.profdef: The quadratic tabulation for Longest Increasing Subsequence fills an array where each cell holds the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at that index. Each cell is one plus the maximum length among all earlier indices with a smaller value, defaulting to one. Predecessor pointers recorded during the fill let us walk back and reconstruct the actual elements, not just the length.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India not only wants the longest run of strictly rising monthly balances but also wants to list exactly which months formed that run, so analysts can point to the specific improving months in a credit report.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each cell is one plus the best smaller-earlier cell, and predecessor links rebuild the actual run.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The quadratic tabulation for Longest Increasing Subsequence fills an array where each cell holds the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at that index. Each cell is one plus the maximum length among all earlier indices with a smaller value, defaulting to one. Predecessor pointers recorded during the fill let us walk back and reconstruct the actual elements, not just the length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India not only wants the longest run of strictly rising monthly balances but also wants to list exactly which months formed that run, so analysts can point to the specific improving months in a credit report.

**One line to remember:** Each cell is one plus the best smaller-earlier cell, and predecessor links rebuild the actual run.

sections.s2_technical:
We create a length array where every entry starts at one, because any single element is an increasing subsequence of length one. For each index i we scan all earlier indices j, and whenever the value at j is smaller than the value at i and the length at j plus one beats the current length at i, we update the length at i and record j as the predecessor of i. We track the overall best length and the index where it ends. To reconstruct, we follow predecessor links from that ending index back to the start, collecting values, then reverse them.

The fill core is `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { len[i] = 1; prev[i] = -1; for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) if (nums[j] < nums[i] && len[j] + 1 > len[i]) { len[i] = len[j] + 1; prev[i] = j; } }`. A concrete check: with balances 3, 4, 1, 5 the length array becomes 1, 2, 1, 3 and following predecessors from the last index yields 3, 4, 5. Senior nuance: this is order n squared time and linear space, slower than the n log n patience method, but it reconstructs the actual subsequence very naturally, which the binary-search method does not do without extra bookkeeping.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants not just the length of the longest strictly rising run of monthly balances but the exact months that formed it, so a credit report can cite the specific improving months. The length alone is not enough; analysts need the actual sequence. This is exactly how the quadratic tabulation with predecessor pointers works: it builds lengths bottom-up and reconstructs the real run.

The code defines a `CreditTrendService` with `longestRisingSequence(balances)` returning the actual rising values. A `Demo` provides monthly balances and logs the reconstructed run.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is monthly balances three, four, one, five. Step 1: we set all lengths to one and all predecessors to minus one. Step 2: at index one, value four, we look back at index zero, value three; since three is smaller, length one becomes two and its predecessor becomes zero. Step 3: at index two, value one, no earlier value is smaller, so it stays length one with no predecessor. Step 4: at index three, value five, we look back and find index one, value four, gives the best extension, so length three becomes three and its predecessor becomes one. Step 5: the best length is three ending at index three. Step 6: we follow predecessors from index three to one to zero, collecting five, four, three, then reverse to get three, four, five as the reconstructed rising run.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:43:15 PM com.bank.credittrend.service.CreditTrendService longestRisingSequence
INFO: Longest rising run of balances = [3, 4, 5]
Oct 27, 2026 9:43:15 PM com.bank.credittrend.CreditTrendApplication main
INFO: Final reconstructed run = [3, 4, 5]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: balances = [3, 4, 1, 5]   indices 0..3
    │
    ▼
  len=[1,1,1,1]  prev=[-1,-1,-1,-1]
    ▼ i=1(4): 3<4 → len[1]=2, prev[1]=0
    ▼ i=2(1): none smaller → len[2]=1
    ▼ i=3(5): 4<5 best → len[3]=3, prev[3]=1
    │
    ▼  bestLen=3, bestEnd=3
  reconstruct: 3 ← prev1 ← prev0  collect [5,4,3] reverse
    │
    ▼
  Output: [3, 4, 5]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The quadratic tabulation for the Longest Increasing Subsequence is the version I reach for when I need the actual elements, not merely the length. I keep a length array where each entry holds the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at that index, and I start every entry at one because a single element is itself an increasing subsequence. For each index I scan all earlier indices, and whenever an earlier value is smaller and extending its run would beat my current best, I update my length and record that earlier index as my predecessor.

The predecessor array is what makes reconstruction clean. After the fill I know the best overall length and the index where it ends, so I follow the predecessor links backward from that ending index, collecting each value, and then reverse the collected list to put it in forward order. This is order n squared time and linear space, which is slower than the n log n patience-sorting method, but it reconstructs the real subsequence naturally, whereas the binary-search method only gives the length without extra bookkeeping.

At the National Bank of India I used this when a credit report needed to cite the exact months during which a customer's balance strictly rose, not just how many such months there were. I ran the quadratic fill over the monthly balances and followed the predecessor chain to produce the actual list of improving months. Explaining the length-ending-here definition, the predecessor links, and the trade-off against the faster method that cannot easily reconstruct is what shows an interviewer I understand both the computation and the recovery of the answer.
